text: By the time we arrived, the train ___.
why: B1 past perfect, too easy for B2; 'was leaving' also works (train was just pulling out)

text: She’s the woman ___ helped me yesterday.
why: A2 relative pronoun, too easy for B2

text: You ___ smoke here; it is not allowed.
why: A2/B1 mustn't vs don't have to, too easy for B2

text: If I ___ you, I would apologise.
why: B1 fixed phrase 'If I were you', too easy for B2

text: The package ___ tomorrow morning.
why: B1 future passive, too easy for B2

text: The committee recommended that the rules ___ revised.
why: Subjunctive after recommend: BrE also accepts 'were revised' (and 'should be'); British/American difference decides

text: He has worked here since three years.
why: since/for is an A2/B1 point, too easy for B2

text: The problem must to be solved today.
why: must + to is an A2/B1 error, too easy for B2

text: She suggested me to try again.
why: One part is an empty string (not in the sentence); explanation relies on the US-style subjunctive 'that I try'

text: She decided to ___ up smoking last year.
why: 'take up smoking' is also correct and natural

text: The meeting was ___ off because of the storm.
why: 'put off' (postponed) is also correct

text: He wants to ___ for a new position at work.
why: 'ask for a new position' is also acceptable

text: The instructions were very ___. (CONFUSE)
why: 'confused' (= muddled, unclear) also fits instructions (Cambridge: 'The instructions were rather confused'); answer lacks it

text: This decision was completely ___. (REASON)
why: 'reasonable' is equally correct; answer lists only 'unreasonable'

text: The furniture in the office are very old.
why: One part is an empty string (not in the sentence)

text: The problem was difficult to be solved.
why: Empty part; explanation 'after a difficult noun' is garbled (should be: after difficult/easy + to, use the active infinitive)

text: He suggested that she takes a break.
why: 'suggested that she takes/took' is acceptable in British English; British/American difference decides

text: I would rather you don’t tell anyone.
why: 'would rather you + present' is used informally; would-rather-you point is on the excluded list

text: The number of problems have decreased significantly.
why: One part is an empty string (not in the sentence)

text: The team decided to ___ back the release date.
why: 'put back' (= postpone, BrE) is also correct

text: They want to ___ down the old warehouse.
why: 'bring down' / 'take down' a building are also used for demolishing

text: His behaviour at the meeting was highly ___. (PROFESSION)
why: 'professional' ('highly professional') is equally correct; answer lists only 'unprofessional'

text: She suggested that he ___ the report before Friday.
why: 'submitted' (and 'should submit') is correct in British English; subjunctive difference decides

text: The package ___ by the courier tomorrow.
why: B1 future passive, too easy for B2

text: I’d rather you ___ anyone about the change yet.
why: 'don’t tell' is used informally; would-rather-you point is on the excluded list

text: The company has been ___ to reduce costs this year.
why: Present perfect continuous form is B1, too easy for B2

text: The new system is much ___ than the old one.
why: A2 comparative, too easy for B2

text: She has worked here since five years.
why: since/for is an A2/B1 point, too easy for B2

text: If I will see her, I will give her the message.
why: First conditional 'will' after if is a B1 point, too easy for B2

text: The number of applicants have increased this year.
why: One part is an empty string (not in the sentence)

text: We need to ___ down the main points before writing the report.
why: 'write down', 'put down' and 'take down' are all also correct

text: She managed to ___ over a difficult period at work.
why: 'get over a period' is unnatural (you get through a period, get over an illness/loss)

text: He wants to ___ for a management position.
why: 'ask for a management position' is also acceptable

text: The instructions were very ___. (CONFUSE)
why: 'confused' (= muddled, unclear) also fits instructions; answer lacks it

text: The decision seemed completely ___. (REASON)
why: 'reasonable' is equally correct; answer lists only 'unreasonable'
